overview: The exact atlas record labels one approximate 1492 to 1500 polygon “Inupiat.” It should be read as a snapshot, not a surveyed border, population map, or centralized state. The shape includes Utqiagvik, Nuiqsut, Kaktovik, Anaktuvuk Pass, Noatak, Shungnak, and even Unalakleet, yet excludes Point Hope, Wainwright, Kotzebue, Kivalina, Wales, Shishmaref, Teller, and Nome. It overlaps other atlas layers. Iñupiat names the people collectively; Iñupiaq can name one person, the language, or serve adjectivally. Regional communities and language varieties remain distinct, as do Siberian Yupik neighbors, Canadian Inuvialuit, organizations, and archaeological labels such as Birnirk, Western Thule, and Kotzebue. Archaeology around Wales, Cape Krusenstern, Point Hope, Walakpa, and Cape Espenberg supplies varied histories rather than a founding year. Houses, boats, clothing, whaling, food sharing, family ties, navigation, teaching, art, care, water, and waste practices must be dated and sourced separately. The eight one-year periods below are slices of the sole atlas interval, not annual revolutions. The exact id disappears in 1500 and a separate inupiaq id appears in 1530; Iñupiat communities did not vanish between map files and continue today.

periods.title: The atlas opens one approximate snapshot
periods.summary: The repository first paints the exact inupiat id in 1492, but no historical source identifies an event that year which created Iñupiat people or fixed their homeland. This annual band is an editorial slice of one approximate map interval, not a dated political accession or migration.

periods.title: Kotzebue archaeology crosses the map date
periods.summary: Cape Krusenstern interpretation labels Kotzebue archaeological materials broadly from 1400 to 1700 and documents changing semi-subterranean houses. That long band crosses 1493 without recording a yearly turning point. Archaeological labels help order material patterns; they are not alternate names for every Iñupiat community.

periods.title: Regional histories resist one uniform chronology
periods.summary: Wales preserves archaeology from Birnirk phases onward and occupies a cross-strait position reachable by skin boat. Those sequences demonstrate long interaction and local variation. They do not establish that every northern Alaskan settlement changed together in 1494, so this band remains a cautious narrative division.

periods.title: Coastal settlement remains dynamic
periods.summary: Cape Krusenstern research finds environmental change, uneven preservation, and a population increase continuing until roughly five hundred years ago. That broad archaeological pattern approaches the atlas interval without pinpointing 1495. A changing coast can preserve, erase, or rearrange evidence as well as influence human choices.

periods.title: House deposits preserve activities selectively
periods.summary: A Cape Espenberg house predating this interval contained plant remains in living, roof, fill, and midden contexts. Researchers stress formation processes, trampling, cleaning, dumping, and later movement. The lesson for 1496 is methodological: a seed’s location needs context before it becomes a meal, roof, or child’s activity.

periods.title: Bering Strait links places without merging peoples
periods.summary: At Wales, sequential sites and the short sea crossing toward Chukotka record a connected region. Travel and exchange could move materials, skills, stories, and relationships while communities remained distinct. Nothing in the evidence turns 1497 into a centralized frontier or makes archaeological phase names living ethnic labels.

periods.title: Knowledge travels through observation and practice
periods.summary: Community-reviewed Bering Strait work explains that current, ice, wind, weather, and animal knowledge is place-specific and taught through experienced people. Its modern testimony documents living expertise, not a transcript from 1498. It nevertheless shows why a polygon cannot substitute for learned routes, warnings, and responsibilities.

periods.title: The exact id ends while people continue
periods.summary: At 1500 the exact inupiat feature disappears, then a separate inupiaq id appears in 1530. The twenty-year gap and spelling change belong to atlas classification. They do not prove disappearance, replacement, or a cultural fall, and no automatic successor is asserted between distinct repository records.

items.text: The exact id is inupiat, displayed “Inupiat,” with one approximate 1492 to 1500 interval. Coverage calls it a state, yet no card or override supports that classification. Its imported description sketches modern territory. This packet keeps the id but presents diverse Iñupiat communities as a culture, without inventing a centralized government.

All fifty border snapshots were decoded. The target occurs once, only in world-1492.json, as one polygon with one ring and 183 positions. Its bounds run from about 168.1811 degrees west to 133.7215 west and 63.8449 north to 71.3545 north. Precision one is source metadata, not survey accuracy.

Utqiagvik, Kaktovik, Nuiqsut, Anaktuvuk Pass, Noatak, Shungnak, and Unalakleet test inside. Point Hope, Wainwright, Kotzebue, Kivalina, Selawik, Wales, Shishmaref, Teller, and Nome test outside. A homeland map excluding that many core places has volunteered to wear its own warning label.

The target shares decoded arcs with yup-ik-cup-ik and inuvialuit and has positive-area overlap candidates including Koyukon, Gwich’in, Denendeh, Inuvialuit, and Yup’ik layers. At Anaktuvuk Pass and Shungnak, representative points have several owners. These are topology facts, not permissions to merge identities or territories.

The exact id is absent in 1400, appears in 1492, and is absent in 1500. A separate exact inupiaq feature begins in 1530. Those abrupt switches reveal atlas editing and spelling categories. They do not date the arrival, departure, renaming, or political submission of Iñupiat communities.

Cape Krusenstern researchers call Western Thule, roughly 1000 to 1400, and Kotzebue, roughly 1400 to 1700, archaeological cultures. Both are analytical groupings built from sites and artifacts. They should not be substituted mechanically for the name, boundaries, language, or self-identification of every Iñupiat community.

Wales sites span Birnirk phases to the present and helped archaeologists define successive precontact northern Alaskan patterns. “Birnirk” names an archaeological pattern, not a nation that can be drawn as this polygon. Living Iñupiat histories at Wales continue beyond any one excavated layer or typology.

Cape Krusenstern’s beach ridges preserve sites in a time-ordered coastal landscape, but erosion and deposition change what survives. A reported population increase until about five hundred years ago is a regional reconstruction, not an exact count for 1492. Missing sites and missing people are not the same thing.

The coastal settlement brief reports nearly continuous occupation across two millennia despite environmental variability. Continuity here means recurring human use documented by survey, not one unchanged village, population, or custom. Archaeologists ask how people adapted; the evidence does not authorize a frozen portrait of “traditional life.”

A Point Hope thesis remapped Ipiutak burials and found four construction types across at least five centuries. Taphonomy and changing mortuary behavior explained much variation better than simple gender or rank. Ipiutak is an earlier archaeological tradition, not a synonym for the Iñupiat of 1492.

sections.title: Follow distinct regions, seasons, and routes

items.text: A National Park Service overview describes seasonal movement with food availability and records how an outsider once mistook a normal shortage for chronic starvation. That caution matters: mobility can be planned expertise, and a lean moment cannot stand for every household, season, inland group, or coastal community.

The Alaska Eskimo Whaling Commission represents eleven bowhead-whaling communities, including Iñupiat villages and the Siberian Yupik communities of Gambell and Savoonga. Its list demonstrates shared work alongside different identities. “Arctic whaler” is therefore not a safe shortcut that erases language, island, coast, or regional history.

The modern Iñupiat Community of the Arctic Slope describes eight member communities across coast, river delta, and Brooks Range settings. It is a present tribal government, not the authority behind a 1492 state. Its geography demonstrates real diversity that the imported polygon and singular state label conceal.

Kawerak participants from Wales, Shishmaref, and Diomede explain currents that change with tide, wind, season, ice, and local channels. The book warns readers to consult experts in their own community. Navigation knowledge is geographically precise even when the atlas is not, and expertise cannot be generalized carelessly.

Systematic survey at Cape Krusenstern records changing intensity of coastal occupation rather than a single permanent boundary. Long use amid environmental variability shows resilience as a research question, not a slogan. Communities made choices among coast, lagoon, river, and interior opportunities at different times and scales.

sections.title: Coordinate food, whaling, sharing, and care

items.text: A government environmental review describes bowhead hunting as concentrated community-wide work requiring knowledge of ice, weather, and whale behavior. Captains supported crews and were respected for generosity and stewardship. The report documents modern formalized patterns and long continuity; it does not provide a crew roster from 1492.

The Commission’s village accounts pair bowhead hunting with walrus, seals, birds, fish, crab, and terrestrial resources. The mix differs by place. Coastal Iñupiat life cannot be reduced to one whale, while inland Nunamiut histories require still different emphasis. A menu assembled for everyone would be historically overcooked.

At contemporary Nalukataq celebrations, the whole community participates and whale meat and maktak are shared, with portions saved for later gatherings. This community source establishes living responsibility and transmission. It is not evidence that every detail, date, serving order, or festival form was identical in the fifteenth century.

Current Point Hope whaling observations link sea-ice conditions with inherited knowledge and community reporting. They show that subsistence combines food, travel safety, observation, and teaching. Because equipment, climate, and regulations change, the page supports continuity of expertise rather than a claim that today reenacts 1492 unchanged.

The Alaska Eskimo Whaling Commission speaks for both Iñupiat and Siberian Yupik member villages and centers bowhead stewardship. This modern co-management organization did not exist in 1492. Its work belongs in the continuity story, where adapting institutions protect relationships and harvesting rights without collapsing distinct peoples into one identity.

sections.title: Build houses, clothing, boats, tools, and art

items.text: Kotzebue-period houses at Cape Krusenstern were dug partly below ground, framed with wood, and covered with skins, sod, or gravel. Shape and construction varied over time. These remains demonstrate cold-climate engineering, but a house outline rarely identifies every resident, sleeping place, repairer, or conversation once held inside.

A Cape Espenberg dwelling preserves plant remains differently in its living surface, roof fall, fill, and midden. Sweeping, trampling, dumping, children’s activity, decay, and later movement may alter deposits. Archaeobotany can illuminate plant use only when context survives, so seeds are clues rather than an automatic pantry list.

A Smithsonian guide records layered caribou-skin clothing, gut waterproofing, and women’s larger hoods for carrying small children. An Iñupiat doll maker recalled girls practicing parka construction on dolls. These later teachings illuminate material skill and childhood learning, while designs and roles still require place and date labels.

Alaska’s Sheldon Jackson Museum groups Iñupiat and Yupik collections separately while listing gut and skin clothing, kayaks, masks, baskets, ivory, bone, and driftwood objects. Scarce trees made salvaged wood valuable. Museum categories and surviving objects reveal materials, but not a complete household inventory for 1492.

A Smithsonian mask combines spruce, caribou teeth, a thanksgiving setting, and images of whaling crews in umiaks. It joins art, animals, boats, and ceremony in one object. The undated web description cannot be assigned to 1492, so the mask appears as cultural continuity, not a calendar anchor.

sections.title: See families, women, children, elders, and community

items.text: Murdoch’s 1881 to 1883 Point Barrow observations describe widespread adoption, care for orphans, and children treated as full family members. This is valuable later testimony, filtered through a colonial male observer nearly four centuries after the atlas date. It documents possibilities and continuity, not universal 1492 household rules.

The same late source says wives were consulted on important household decisions and older women held precedence in their work, while village matters were discussed informally and elders’ opinions carried weight. Its language and assumptions require scrutiny. No one observer can turn local nineteenth-century practice into a timeless constitution.

Ublasaun history names extended kin, an adopted son, widowed and married households, and seasonal dispersal from a small twentieth-century settlement. It also notes women healers and midwives at Shishmaref. These named lives correct generic family sketches, while their dates prevent backward projection into 1492.

A current ICAS plan names family and kinship, love and respect for elders, cooperation, sharing, language, compassion, and humor among guiding Iñupiat values. The list is community-authored modern evidence. It helps frame continuity but does not prove identical wording, institutions, or expectations in every earlier community.

Point Hope burial research warns that grave variation may reflect time and preservation rather than simple gender or status. That restraint protects women, men, and children from being sorted into confident social roles by objects alone. Mortuary evidence needs context, and a burial population is never a complete village census.

sections.title: Learn through language, observation, stories, and practice

items.text: Paul Ongtooguk describes traditional Iñupiat education through observation, stories, disciplined practice, apprenticeship, camp chores, and environmental judgment. The community itself could be a school. This published reflection explains a teaching system, but the card still avoids inventing a timetable, enrollment list, or standardized classroom in 1492.

Bering Strait experts stress learning currents from elders and experienced travelers, preferably in the boat and on the ice. The Kawerak book says written guidance cannot replace one-to-one teaching. Words, routes, weather, judgment, and responsibility develop together; reading a map alone does not make someone safe.

ICAS now builds education around Iñupiaq language, culture, Qargi Academy, teacher apprenticeships, community partnerships, and learning from childhood through adulthood. These are modern tribal programs, not reconstructed fifteenth-century schools. They demonstrate active educational sovereignty and living change rather than survival as a museum display.

UAF describes four North Slope and Seward Peninsula dialect types in two larger groups and credits named speakers and elders who refined a major lexicon. “Iñupiaq” can name the language, while Iñupiat names the people collectively. Dialect diversity makes one undifferentiated atlas label especially misleading.

Secure modern sample, already in Latin orthography: “Aarigaa, iñupiallaaruni suli kaniqsiļļaruni. Iļisaġiaġin!” The North Slope Borough translates it, “It’s good to speak and understand the language. Come and Learn!” No transliteration is added, and this is not passed off as a 1492 inscription.

sections.title: Discuss health, healing, birth, risk, and care honestly

items.text: Murdoch’s late Point Barrow account records both men and women recognized as healers, ritual treatment, scarification, rough surgery, and one reported plant or turf medicine. The observer admitted difficulty obtaining information. These pages document nineteenth-century encounters, not a complete medical system or a treatment manual for 1492.

The Ublasaun history identifies Shishmaref as a place where Iñupiat women healers and midwives assisted childbirth in the early twentieth century. It securely supports women’s care work in that later setting. It cannot supply a fifteenth-century birth procedure, medicine list, or claim that all communities organized care alike.

Present ICAS community services include elder respite, help with housework and meals, child and family support, scholarships, and burial assistance. These programs show care adapting through a tribal government. They belong to modern continuity and should not be renamed as precontact institutions merely because their concerns are familiar.

The current ICAS development plan treats children, elders, health, mental health, food security, recreation, culture, and safety as connected community priorities. That holistic organization is contemporary evidence. It encourages a broad view of well-being without licensing a specific diagnosis, healer title, or remedy for 1492.

Reviewed fifteenth-century archaeological sources preserve houses, plants, tools, burials, and settlement patterns, but no named patient, healer, midwife, diagnosis, or securely dated prescription from 1492 to 1500. People certainly managed illness and injury; the local details remain an evidence gap rather than an invitation to import generic Arctic medicine.

sections.title: Address water, hygiene, refuse, and toilets without guessing

items.text: Murdoch reports that late nineteenth-century Point Barrow winter houses economized scarce water, scraped floors and walls, used indoor vessels, and discarded mixed human waste outdoors. He also describes varied washing practices. This is direct but late and judgment-laden testimony, not proof of an identical sanitation routine in 1492.

ANTHC’s current Kivalina project replaces honey buckets with a low-flow sink and toilet, treats stored rain, melted ice, or hauled river water, separates wastewater, and manages dried solids. Its modern engineering answers present health needs. It must not be smuggled backward as evidence for fifteenth-century plumbing.

The same tribal health source connects adequate household water with handwashing, cleaning, hygiene, and reduced exposure to human waste. More than thirty remote Alaska communities still lack system-wide plumbing. That present inequality warns against romantic claims that Arctic adaptation made sanitation effortless, uniform, or historically static.

Cape Krusenstern houses and the Cape Espenberg dwelling provide architecture, floor deposits, roof fall, and midden contexts, but the reviewed studies identify no latrine, toilet, sewer, drain, or standardized human-waste facility securely dated to 1492 to 1500. Absence in this evidence set is reported narrowly.

Archaeological survey finds hearths, house depressions, camps, and storage features through systematic recording. A pit becomes a toilet only when context and contents support that function. Convenient shape is not enough. For this interval, the toilet detectives have a clipboard, excellent boots, and no confirmed facility.

sections.title: Recognize achievements and close the atlas seam carefully

items.text: Wales archaeology and the short Bering Strait crossing show generations of boat travel and exchange before European mapping. NPS notes that local peoples already knew lands and trading partners across the water. This achievement joined navigation, weather judgment, craft, language, and diplomacy without requiring one trans-strait empire.

Cape Krusenstern chronology and settlement research demonstrate long use of a changing coast, durable winter architecture, and adaptation across environmental variability. The achievement is sustained community life through skilled choices, not a frozen “survival” tableau. Archaeological culture names remain tools for analysis rather than identities imposed on descendants.

The Smithsonian’s Iñupiat ceremonial-mask record and its Crossroads exhibition page place masks within a wider museum record of kayaks, harpoons, ivory carvings, beadwork, drums, clothing, journals, and photographs. Objects document art and skilled work, while exhibition selection limits what a label can recover; community knowledge remains essential to interpretation.

North Slope Borough programs update a Traditional Land Use Inventory, preserve oral histories and life histories, care for collections, and support elders teaching young people. These modern institutions distinguish community authority from the atlas. They also show why living knowledge should guide interpretation of old maps and excavated objects.

At the endpoint, inupiat disappears from the atlas; the separate inupiaq id does not appear until 1530. No conquest, migration, epidemic, or cultural ending is documented at that seam. Iñupiat communities continued, and present institutions still teach language, sustain whaling, care for families, and govern changing responsibilities.

ending.text: The exact inupiat feature ends at 1500 because the atlas changes its categories, not because Iñupiat people fell, migrated away, or stopped speaking their language. The next snapshot has no exact feature, and a separate inupiaq id begins only in 1530. No automatic predecessor or successor is asserted across that software gap. Archaeological sequences, community histories, and living institutions instead show continuity with change: regional settlements, family and crew relationships, whaling and other harvesting, travel knowledge, art, teaching, care, and language endured while practices and organizations adapted. Today the Alaska Eskimo Whaling Commission protects bowhead relationships and rights, and the North Slope Borough teaches an exact modern Iñupiatun welcome: “Aarigaa, iñupiallaaruni suli kaniqsiļļaruni. Iļisaġiaġin!” This later sample is living-language evidence, not a fifteenth-century text. The atlas interval closes; Iñupiat peoplehood does not.
